extracted.intended_audience: The People of the State of New York; citizens considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century Federalist essay explaining and defending the specific powers granted to the general government and the prohibitions placed on the States by the proposed U.S. Constitution, with justifications and practical consequences. It analyzes miscellaneous federal powers, guarantees to States, prior debts, amendment/ratification rules, and restraints on state authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to coin money and regulate its value (including foreign coin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to coin money, regulate the value thereof, and of foreign coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains necessity: uniformity of current coin value would be destroyed if foreign coin were subject to differing state regulations; Congress's authority is limited to coin struck by their own authority or that of the States. Prevents multiple currencies, expensive mints, and impediments to interstate commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment of counterfeiting public securities and current coin
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment of counterfeiting the public securities, as well as the current coin, is submitted to the national authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Couples the punishment with the power to secure the value of both coin and securities; presented as a natural incident of the monetary power to preserve public credit and currency integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of weights and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to regulate weights and measures transferred from the Articles of Confederation to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founded on same considerations as coinage — uniform standards facilitate commerce and inter-state intercourse; an improvement over the Confederation's approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform rule of naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizing the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses defects of the Confederation where disparate state naturalization rules could allow persons to evade incapacities by moving between states; uniformity prevents legal contradictions and serious embarrassments (e.g., proscribed persons gaining rights by residence elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform laws of bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely connected to regulation of commerce; prevents frauds where parties or property move across state lines and addresses practical difficulties under the Confederation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribing proof and effect of public acts and judicial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to prescribe by general laws the manner in which public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and the effect they shall have in other States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable improvement over the Confederation's indeterminate clause; convenient instrument of justice especially on borders where effects may be secretly translated into another jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish post roads
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of establishing post roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as harmless and potentially highly convenient; facilitating intercourse between States is a public good deserving public care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote progress of science and useful arts (copyrights & patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to promote the progress of science and useful arts, by securing, for a limited time, to authors and inventors, the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility of the power scarcely questioned; copyright recognized by common law in Britain; inventors' rights likewise reasonable. States cannot separately make effectual provision; federal provision aligns public good with individual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive legislation over federal district and federal places
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To exercise exclusive legislation ... over such district (not exceeding ten miles square) as may ... become the seat of the government of the United States; and ... over all places purchased by the consent of the legislatures of the States ... for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indispensable for complete authority at the seat of government and over federal installations; avoids dependency of federal officers on a single State and prevents state influence. Circumscribed extent and requirement of state concurrence obviate jealousy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to define and punish treason with constrained consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To declare the punishment of treason, but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attained.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress must be able to punish treason against the United States but with constitutional barriers (definition, proof standards) to prevent abuse; limits avoid extending consequences of guilt beyond the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of new States with consent rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to admit new States into the Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the junction of two or more States, or parts of States, without the consent of the legislatures of the States concerned, as well as of the Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplies omitted provision in Confederation; general precaution prevents partitioning of States without consent and quiets jealousy of both larger and smaller States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposal and regulation of United States territory and property (with proviso)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States, with a proviso, that nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular State.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important power required by considerations similar to those for the federal district; proviso proper to address jealousies and claims (e.g., western territory disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantee of republican form and protection of States
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government; to protect each of them against invasion; and on application of the legislature, or of the executive (when the legislature cannot be convened), against domestic violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures federal authority can defend republican institutions and maintain stability; the guaranty does not permit altering republican forms into nonrepublican ones and applies when States request aid or when invasion/domestic violence necessitates interposition; federal interposition is designed to be impartial and preventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of pre-Constitution debts and engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To consider all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of this Constitution, as being no less valid against the United States, under this Constitution, than under the Confederation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory assurance for foreign creditors and public confidence; asserts reciprocal nature of engagements and rebuts fears that a change in political form dissolves moral obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode for amendments and its safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to provide for amendments to be ratified by three fourths of the States under two exceptions only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mode guards against excessive mutability and excessive difficulty; enables both federal and state governments to propose amendments; exceptions protect principles like Senate equality and residuary state sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification rule (nine states sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States, ratifying the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express authority of the people alone could give validity; requiring unanimity would subject essential interests to a single State's caprice; discusses delicate questions about replacing the Confederation and relations between assenting and dissenting States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States making treaties, alliances, confederations, or granting letters of marque
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal;'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copied from the Articles but extended; uniformity in foreign relations is necessary and responsibility should rest with the national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States coining money or issuing bills of credit and limiting legal tender
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No State shall ... coin money; emit bills of credit; make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts;'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents multiplicity of currencies and the pernicious effects of paper money observed after the Revolution; protects interstate commerce and confidence, and avoids economic mischief from unilateral state monetary policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No State shall ... pass any bill of attainder, ex-post-facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts;'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are contrary to principles of social compact and sound legislation; prohibition is a constitutional bulwark for personal security and private rights and guards against legislative interference and speculative abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on granting titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No State shall ... grant any title of nobility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copied from the Articles; intended to prevent aristocratic innovations inconsistent with republicanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on state imposts/duties on imports/exports without Congress consent
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce ... shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraint required to secure uniform trade regulation by the federal government while allowing reasonable discretion for state inspection laws; proceeds of such duties go to the federal treasury and laws are subject to congressional oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on states laying duty on tonnage, maintaining troops/ships in peace, compacts, and war engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects national interests in defense and foreign policy, prevents individual states from independently engaging in measures that could embroil the Union, and reserves coordinated authority to the federal government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to make all laws necessary and proper for carrying into execution constitutional powers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues indispensability of the clause: without it the Constitution would be a dead letter. Discusses alternatives the convention might have used and why they are flawed (strict 'expressly delegated' approach, positive/negative enumerations, silence). Justifies the doctrine that where an end is required the means necessary to that end are authorized; addresses consequences of misconstruction as judicial/political issues resolved as with other powers.
